name: Goldman-style oil demand destruction triangulation during a supply/geopolitical shock
useCases: Estimate near-term oil demand destruction when observed demand is distorted by war, shipping disruption, price spikes, or inventory swings.
Cross-check apparent demand balances against high-frequency retail/product demand indicators.
Separate refined-product demand signals from non-refined petrochemical feedstock demand.
inputs: visible and invisible refined product inventory changes
high-frequency gasoline and diesel demand indicators
IEA/S&P Global/Wood Mackenzie product demand estimates

method.description: Define a no-shock counterfactual path for global oil demand, such as annualized trend growth, before measuring demand destruction.
Estimate apparent refined product demand from refinery runs, product stock changes, product imports and exports, then compare with the counterfactual.
Estimate non-refined demand change separately for LPG, ethane and other petrochemical feedstocks rather than forcing them into refined-product balances.
Build a second estimate from high-frequency demand indicators and retail fuel price changes, applying explicit demand elasticity assumptions where direct data are missing.
Use external forecaster and trading-house estimates as an independent reasonableness check, keeping each institution's number source-labeled.
Present the range and source of disagreement rather than a false precise point estimate; connect price-risk implications separately from the demand estimate.

biasesAndFailureModes: Inventory changes can be mismeasured or lagged, especially invisible stocks.
Retail fuel data can reflect panic buying, rationing, subsidies, mobility restrictions, or reporting distortions rather than underlying consumption.
Elasticity assumptions can dominate estimates outside directly observed regions.
External forecaster averages can create herding if not source-labeled.
A supply shock can raise prices and suppress demand while simultaneously creating bullish price risk, so demand conclusions should not be mechanically mapped to price direction.
historicalCases: 2026 Hormuz shock / Goldman Sachs Oil Comment dated 2026-06-05
automationHooks: Store one observation per method estimate and one forecast record for price-risk framing.
Flag conflicts when EIA, IEA, OPEC, Platts, Argus, or banks publish materially different demand-destruction estimates for the same month.

name: Platts framework for assessing commercial reopening of the Strait of Hormuz
useCases: Evaluate whether Strait of Hormuz can be considered commercially "open" after geopolitical disruption
Assess methodology readiness for resuming Platts MOC assessments requiring Strait transit
Track progress toward normalization across traffic, insurance, security, and fleet deployment dimensions
inputs: tanker type breakdown (crude, product, LPG, LNG vs others)
war risk insurance premium levels and underwriter pool breadth
ceasefire declarations and subsequent attack events
VLCC and large crude carrier deployment into Middle East Gulf
port call and loading program frequency

method.description: Confirm demonstrable sustained ceasefire - no intermittent disruptions for observation period
Measure vessel traffic against pre-war baseline (~135 vessels/day, ~54 tankers/day). Market threshold: 50-90% recovery sustained 1 week to 1 month
Verify minimum observation period of 30-45 days after ceasefire with consistent traffic and no disruptions
Assess marine insurance availability - broad underwriter pool at commercially viable premiums, even if elevated vs pre-war
Confirm physical security: naval mine clearance, functioning maritime security frameworks (patrols, convoys)
Monitor fleet deployment: visible return of VLCCs and large crude carriers, regular port calls, loading programs aligning with pre-war norms

biasesAndFailureModes: Short-lived "open" windows (<24h post-ceasefire, ~48h corridors) can create false positives - require sustained observation
Non-tanker traffic may increase while commercial tanker traffic remains minimal - need to distinguish vessel types
Sanctioned/Iran-linked vessels may distort traffic metrics - country affiliation matters
Behavioral drag: even after conditions met, shipowners/charterers/insurers may delay full return
historicalCases: 2026 Strait of Hormuz crisis (Feb 28 - ongoing as of May 2026)
